title: The halls of memory (Confessions 10.8)
hookLine: Augustine marvels at the vast caverns of memory
tomorrow: after all that searching, where was God the whole time?
last: WE TOUCHED IT FOR A MOMENT.

lines: LILIES AND VIOLETS, IN THE DARK.
WHERE DOES A MIND KEEP IT?
cards: Lilies and violets. In a dark, quiet room, with no flowers anywhere, Augustine can still tell their scents apart. He can call up colors with his eyes shut, and run through a song with his mouth closed.
A phone keeps a camera roll; where does a mind keep all that? That's today's question, and Book Ten of the Confessions turns from his story to the thing that holds his story: memory.

teach.b: He calls it the fields and the wide palaces of memory, storehouses of countless images the senses bring in. And he walks through it like a building. Some things come the moment he asks.
Some take a long search, pulled out of back rooms.
Some rush out in a crowd when he wanted something else, as if asking, is it us you want? He brushes them away with the hand of his heart until the one he's after steps out.
Then the line to tell a friend: people travel far to marvel at mountains, huge waves, long rivers, the ocean and the stars, and they pass themselves by without wonder.
Yet he couldn't even speak of mountains unless he carried them inside. For Augustine, these halls are where his search for God now goes. A neighbor tradition treasures remembering too.
In the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sukhmani Sahib opens, in paraphrase: remember, remember, keep remembering God, and find peace.
Sikhs call this simran. One honest difference: Augustine walks memory's halls asking where God might be found in them; simran remembers God through the Name, repeated again and again.
A search and a remembering, each in its own words.

how: Some Christians end the day by remembering it slowly before God, a practice some traditions call the examen, and Augustine's pages on memory are read as part of that kind of prayer.

games.q: what does “the halls of memory” mean?
o: the vast palace of memory Augustine walks through
a hall in Carthage where he taught speech
a library in Milan where Augustine studied

games.q: the halls of memory — tap the pairs.
p: marvel at mountains, pass themselves by
the Sikh word for remembering God

s: Augustine pictures memory as a small, cramped storeroom
he calls it fields and wide palaces, with countless images.
people travel to marvel at mountains and pass themselves by
Augustine's line in Book Ten: they don't wonder at what's inside.
remembering God is a Christian idea only
Sikhs call it simran: remember, remember, and find peace.

games.q: your friend posts the 'best trip of my life' photos, then admits she barely looked up from her phone. what would Augustine notice?
o: she should have taken more photos, to keep it all.
the wonder lasts when it's taken in, not just on camera.
trips don't matter much, so she shouldn't have gone.
games.why: Augustine: people travel to marvel at mountains and seas, and pass themselves by. the wonder has to be carried inside.

practice: Bring back one good day, any day, and count five things from it, one per breath: a smell, a sound, a color, a taste, a face. Let each come out of the back rooms in its own time.
When you reach five, stay in that day until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: The halls of memory. Augustine's wonder at the palaces inside, where whole mountains and seas are carried.

orig.note: Latin: memory. Augustine speaks of campos et lata praetoria memoriae, the fields and wide palaces of memory, in Confessions 10.8.

carryVoice: Hold this one: the fields of memory, wider than the mountains people cross the world to see. See you soon.
